This is the first page for the discussion of the DDEMESYS protocol (provisional name), a newsgroup like protocol.

I'm pasting the original reddit discussion (aka "first draft"). Further revisions very likely.

Everything's theoretical so far, so if you know of any implementations of something similar, please, do post!

Count me in. I've worked in the past trying to build distributed anonymous P2P services. I'm afraid I can't go into details that without outing my identity. Suffice it to say that I couldn't get anything done due to lack of time :P But well, at least I did a bit of research. I might need to dust off my p2p research skills.

So far what I'm thinking about is a censorship distributed P2P network as the infrastructure (something like Kazaa, I2P, or freenet), and on top of that building our protocol.

My Idea

What reddit currently lacks is the ability to distributedly archive and share past conversations, or threads. (If a thread is deep, it won't be caught by the internet archiver, so the conversation's lost). My idea about sharing is that it won't be entire discussions that will be shared, just threads. And these discussions will be shared a-la P2P, maybe through bittorrent? Whatever the means, these discussions should be able to be shared online and offline, so your discussion program "let's call it "sherrit" as an interim name. (I promise, this interim name won't be permanent or sue its way to the top ;-) )

How to solve this: Instead of having a web server dictate what we read and write, we start with a P2P file sharing protocol, where the files shared are fragments (threads) of discussions. The nodes (servers) aggregate the discussions and allow users to interact with them via a web interface, just like good ol' usenet newsgroups, but this time, we have anonymity and public key encryption and signing. Also, the administrators of a community have power to moderate and ban discussions. However, banned items CAN still be distributed among the servers. Nodes add new replies and post editions when an authorized user submits a reply to an existing discussion.

So, it all starts with a post. What does a post have:

1) ~~Subreddit~~ ahem "Community" id (the founder of a community should have a hierarchical authority, something like a SSL certificate. Maybe it could be refined later to a web of trust?

2) The author's cryptographic ID. This means the author's pseudonym, signed with a public anonymous certificate. The ID can be public, or anonymous. Later, if the author decides, he could certificate the post by certificating the ID's private key and say "Yes, it was me all the time! Shamalamadingdong etc etc". In fact, the author could have multiple identities, and authenticate them as a chain. A warning, tho: Once you've authenticated an identity, there's no turning back. Ideally, you should have a certificate for every single post you make. Sharing public keys with your friends would mean networking anonymously. (Wow, this sounds big... if done correctly, this could take over google plus - but I digress)

3) The original Title, i.e. "DAE herp-a-derp? Karma plz kthx"

4) Time (GMT) when it was posted.

5) The post's cryptographic hash, based on all of the above. In fact, the hash could have all the fields stamped together and attaching the hash after it. i.e. "RedditAlternatives|[insert author's public key]|DAE herp-a-derp? Karma plz kthx|YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS:MMM|[hash of all of the above]"

6) The text body.

7) The author's digitally-signed certificate of the cryptographic hash, to prove he was the one who wrote it.

This would be a distributable "POST". The interesting thing is what comes after.

How replies are stored

For distribution, All replies and edits MUST include a copy of the original post, and ALL the top replies. This means that a 27-level-deep reply includes all the relevant information, up to the original post. For space saving, only the body of the replies and the reference to the previous post's hash can be stored after the end. This is how it would go after packing:

[BEGIN THREAD PACKAGE]
==========================
[POST-PACKAGE, as explained above]
==========================

Reply 1:
==============
Reply-to: [post hash]
[replier's pseudonym Public Key]
[date]
[text body]
==============
[Replier's certificate of the above, let's call it "reply-1-id"]

Reply 2:
==============
Reply-to: [reply-1-id]
[replier 2's pseudonym public key]
[date]
[text body]
==============
[Replier 2's certificate of the above, becomes "reply-2-id"]

Reply 3:
==============
Reply-to: [reply-2-id]
[date]
[etc...]
==============
[/END THREAD PACKAGE]

So, what happens if you want to edit your message? (POST editing is similar)

You add an "Edit package".

EDIT 1:
==============
Edit-for: [reply-N-id]
[your-certificate]
[date]
[text body]
==============
[Your certificate of the above]. Obviously, edits which do not mach the original certificate should be ignore as fraudulent.

Edits might have multiple edit-fors. For example:

EDIT N:
==============
Edit-for: [edit-N-1-id], [edit-N-2-id], [edit-N-3-id], [edit-N-4-id], ... [original-reply-id]
[your-certificate]
[date]
[text body]
==============
[Your certificate of the above]. Obviously, edits which do not mach the original certificate should be ignore as fraudulent.

, so only the latest edit becomes relevant. **In other words, a post for which there's an edit MUST be treated as deprecated, BUT it can be archived to see the history of edits.

So, what do we make of this? That if we have a copy of a thread, or multiple-copies of a relevant thread, gathered from the internet, you can instantly reproduce a copy of the entire discussion.

The good thing is that by packaging the entire thread up to the root (this is, the Original Post), you're avoiding censorship. You can reply to any of the middle discussions, but you can't delete it as if it didn't exist.

For now, you may ask:

HOW TO DELETE MY MESSAGE AND REMAIN ANONYMOUS AFTER A DRUNK REPLY?

The answer is, by captain obvious:

"IF you didn't want your post to be kept for posterity, you shouldn't have replied with your original certificate in the first place!"

See, you'd use a temporary ID, not signed by an official authority (where would this authority come from? That's to be discussed later, I don't have all the answers right now. I'm thinking of a community administrator (that takes place of the reddit mods - this is an upgrade, you're not just a mod, you're an admin!) would grant these userid certificates, so by revoking an author's certificate, the admin would effectively ban the trolls. If only the admin can certificate your ids, this means that there's a strict control of who can post publicly, or anonymously. Admins could grant temporary ids that would expire after a certain date (the certificate would include the expiration date, just like websites https certificates can expire today). After a user proves his worth, his id would get upgraded to a permanent certificate.

Another advantage of this is that your community can't be taken over by another user. What other mods could do, is FORK IT. They would start up their own communities by accepting ids certified by the previous admin.

CENTRALIZED STORAGE (AKA WEBSITES)

What I still haven't thought, is how to distribute the discussions. I'm thinking that the sites could request the users for their threads, and assemble a static page of the discussions.

We could also make it that discussions will expire after say, 2 or 3 months (the poster could maybe add an expiration-date tag, but the permission for adding large discussion expirations should have to be PK-certified by the admin. After the expiration date, the original post couldn't get any more replies, so this would be the perfect way to mark a discussion as "archived".

This can mean that a simple static apache server could store discussions, and those discussions could be redistributed all over the internet.

UPVOTES

Upvotes would be stored in a similar way, something like giving an upvote to a certain post with your public key. I don't see any other way of storing the upvotes (and downvotes) other than with your public key, perhaps using anonymous keys granted by the admins.

... and that's what I have so far.

ANONYMOUS KEYS

1) The registered user requests a pack of keys to the admin. The admin generates a series of certificates, up to 10 per user per day (each certificate would be valid only for a day). Depending on the user's reputation, the admin could grant them for the next 3, 5, 7, 15, or even 30 days. These temporary certificates could be used to participate in discussions anonymously. Since the certificates would be sent encrypted (with the final user's public key for him to decrypt), and since they're limited, there's no risk of an anonymous horde disrupting a discussion.

Admins and netiquette

Admins should never, EVER out a user's certificate. However, he should be able to keep track of which user posts trolling questions, so he could ban the user or just stop giving him anonymous certificates.

Pitfalls

The problem with this scheme is that the admin would have to be available to grant certificates. But if users post using their granted identities, discussions wouldn't need an admin to go on.

How to solve the single-point-of-failure (the admin)? I'm thinking of a web-of-trust, but I haven't researched that so far.
